detail.longDescription: arXiv:2611.33855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Node failures can split an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) network into disconnected groups. Restoring communication requires moving the surviving aircraft, and the operator needs both an executable movement plan and an assessment of how much shorter the recovery could be. We develop Connectivity Restoration Branch-and-Bound (CR-BB), which returns a feasible plan and numerical displacement bounds; dividing these bounds by the common speed gives the corresponding time interval. Exact-arithmetic guarantees are established by the theorems. When the gap is not closed, the plan is feasible but not certified optimal. A fixed-tree subproblem is a second-order cone program. CR-BB searches over spanning trees and uses a Joint Mandatory-Link Bound (JMLB) to remove tree families that cannot improve the incumbent; Progress-based Adaptive Stopping (PAS) controls the search budget. On 200 matched cases, enabling the JMLB in the branch bound raised the number of cases meeting the prescribed displacement gap from 182 to 200 and reduced mean expanded nodes from 49.6 to 0.7. On a 60-case exact comparison, CR-BB met the gap in 90.0% of cases, compared with 55.0% for a spanning-tree mixed-integer conic formulation and 37.5% of the eight runs completed by an independent optimizer. On 1,000 paired recovery cases, CR-BB planned first restored connectivity in 72.35 steps on average, compared with 124.32 for an edge-augmentation baseline with conic refinement, a 41.8% reduction; on the common 50% subset the reduction was 28.1%. Across 2,466 cases, PAS reduced cumulative solver time by 20.9% and expanded nodes by 31.1% relative to a fixed search budget, with a 0.36-step mean increase in planned steps; most of the saving came from cases where neither configuration met the gap, and 60 plans became longer.
